title: Donald Trump and China President Xi Jinping Want Jensen Back at Nvidia!
author: B
text:
Daniel Nenni
Founder
Staff member

President Donald Trump said Friday that Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang should apologize and return as chief executive, publicly backing his reinstatement days after the chipmaker’s board rejected the idea. Trump also said he discussed Huang with Chinese President Xi Jinping during his trip to Asia this week.

Speaking at a White House news conference, Trump said he wanted Huang to “make a big apology” and go back to Nvidia. He praised Huang’s role in building the company and said Xi shared his assessment of Huang’s abilities. Trump gave few details about their discussion.

Nvidia announced Huang’s resignation on Nov. 12 and appointed Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as interim CEO. Kress will continue to serve as CFO while the board considers internal and external candidates for the permanent job. Longtime director Harvey C. Jones was named board chair.

Huang said Tuesday he would be willing to return if asked and pledged to cooperate with the board’s independent investigation. Jones told investors that directors had unanimously accepted Huang’s resignation and did not intend to reinstate him. Trump’s remarks put the president at odds with the position Nvidia’s board laid out earlier this week.

The leadership dispute comes amid scrutiny of U.S. chip export enforcement. House Democrats have asked Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick for records and answers by Dec. 1 about Nvidia’s contacts with officials investigating whether Singapore-based cloud company Megaspeed diverted chips to China. Megaspeed says it complies with U.S. export controls. The Commerce and Justice departments said the federal investigation began in 2024 and that Justice later took the lead in the criminal inquiry.

Trump also said Friday that he still supports Lutnick, who faces questions over his handling of chip sales to China. The United States restricts shipments of its most advanced chips to China, placing Nvidia at the center of a policy debate over Beijing’s access to computing power for artificial intelligence.
